questions.question: Q: What is the advantage of using a tally chart when collecting data?

points.text: A tally chart allows data to be recorded quickly and efficiently as it is collected, and the grouped tally marks (every five) make counting easy.

questions.question: Q: Data is recorded in the grouped frequency table with class intervals 0–9, 10–19, 20–29. What is the class width of each interval?

points.text: Each class interval has a width of 10. For the interval 0–9, the boundaries are –0.5 and 9.5, giving a width of 10.

questions.question: Q: In a two-way table, 40 students study Biology, 30 study Chemistry, and 15 study both. How many study at least one subject?

points.text: Using the addition rule: 40 + 30 – 15 = 55 students study at least one subject.

Full-Mark Response A survey of 60 households recorded the number of pets owned. The results are shown in the grouped frequency table below. Estimate the mean number of pets. Class intervals: 0–2 (f=22), 2–4 (f=18), 4–6 (f=12), 6–8 (f=8) <div class="

points.text: Class interval | Midpoint (m) | Frequency (f) | f x m 0 ≤ x < 2 | 1 | 22 | 22 2 ≤ x < 4 | 3 | 18 | 54 4 ≤ x < 6 | 5 | 12 | 60 6 ≤ x < 8 | 7 | 8 | 56 Total | | 60 | 192 Estimated mean = Σ(fm) ÷ Σf = 192 ÷ 60 = 3.2 pets. The mean is estimated because we use midpoints rather than the actual data values within each class.
